displayQuote: Even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise

meta.title: Who really said "Even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Victor Hugo — this line is from Herbert Kretzmer's 1985 Les Misérables stage-musical Finale, not the 1862 novel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Victor Hugo, but the line is really from Herbert Kretzmer's 1985 Les Misérables musical lyrics.

answer.label: Not Victor Hugo — actually Herbert Kretzmer
answer.sourceLine: This line does not appear in Hugo’s 1862 novel. It was written by lyricist Herbert Kretzmer for the Finale of the 1985 English-language stage adaptation of Les Misérables, and has since spread online as a direct Hugo quotation.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: For the wretched of the earth there is a flame that never dies; even the darkest night will end and the sun will rise.
trail: First documented as a line from the Finale of the 1985 English-language stage musical, credited to lyricist Herbert Kretzmer on Wikiquote ↗.
Two blogs dedicated to correcting this exact myth, This is not a Victor Hugo quote ↗ and Incorrect(ly Attributed) Les Mis Quotes ↗, independently trace the line to Kretzmer’s musical-only lyrics.
Despite this, the line circulates widely as a direct Victor Hugo quotation, for instance on Goodreads ↗.
Even a Sotheby’s listing ↗ for a genuine 1862 first edition of the novel used the line as marketing copy, though it appears nowhere in the book being sold.
source.excerptNote: Some lyric transcriptions render this as “darkest nights” (plural); Wikiquote’s sourced text uses the singular “darkest night,” matching the popular quotation.
source.rightsHolder: Herbert Kretzmer (lyrics) and the Les Misérables stage-production rights holders (Cameron Mackintosh Ltd. / Alain Boublil Music Ltd.)
source.rightsNote: This exact English line comes from Kretzmer’s 1985 stage-musical lyrics, which remain under copyright. It is not a line from Hugo’s public-domain 1862 novel, so no public-domain claim applies to this wording.

author.name: Herbert Kretzmer
author.heading: About Herbert Kretzmer
author.bio: Kretzmer was a South African-born journalist who became a leading London theatre critic before turning lyricist. His English-language lyrics for the 1985 stage adaptation of Les Misérables — built on Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel’s French original, with music by Claude-Michel Schönberg — won him a Tony Award and a Grammy.

misattribution.heading: The Novel/Musical Mix-Up
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most common Les Misérables mix-ups: a line written fresh for the stage musical gets credited to the novel’s author.

items.why: The line is absent from Hugo’s 1862 novel; it was composed by Herbert Kretzmer specifically for the musical’s Finale, per Wikiquote’s sourced lyrics ↗.
Even a Sotheby’s listing ↗ for a genuine first edition of the novel used the line as a headline, without it appearing in the book itself.

misattribution.truthLine: The words belong to lyricist Herbert Kretzmer ↗, written for the 1985 English-language Les Misérables stage musical — not to Victor Hugo’s novel.

context.heading: Why It Endures
lead: The line closes the musical’s Finale, sung as the ensemble reprises the show’s themes after Jean Valjean’s death — a moment of collective hope rather than a passage lifted from Hugo’s prose.

Because the 1985 stage adaptation shares its title and characters with Hugo’s 1862 novel, lines written fresh for the show are routinely mistaken for the novelist’s own words — this is one of the most widely shared examples of that mix-up.
detailsBody: Kretzmer’s English lyrics, adapted from Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel’s original French libretto (music by Claude-Michel Schönberg), expanded the show for its 8 October 1985 Barbican Theatre opening and won him a Tony Award and a Grammy.
context.pull: It’s a wonderful line, and well in keeping with the story, but it’s not a Hugo quote.
